expected_findings.description: `update` is no longer atomic. It reads the current value through `get`, which takes and releases the map lock, runs the closure with no lock held, and then takes the lock a second time to store the result. Any other thread that modifies the same key inside that window has its write overwritten by the stale-derived value. Because `add` is implemented on top of `update`, every counter increment in the crate inherits the lost-update window: two concurrent `add` calls on one key can leave the counter as though only one of them happened.

notes:
Constructed by turning an atomic read-modify-write under one guard into a read, an unguarded computation, and a separate write. The evidence needed to see it is entirely inside the diff plus the two-line body of `get` a few lines above; no cross-file investigation is required.

Why the shipped suite misses it: all four tests in src/counters.rs are single-threaded. A lost update requires a second thread to complete a whole `update` inside the window between the first thread's read and its write, and no test creates a second thread at all. Single-threaded, the read and the write are never separated by anyone else's work, so `add_accumulates` and `update_stores_the_computed_value` observe exactly the same results before and after the change.

The change's stated rationale is genuine, not a fig leaf: the pre-change version does hold a non-reentrant `Mutex` across arbitrary caller code. The fix is to keep the operation atomic some other way (a re-check-and-retry loop, or documenting that the closure must not re-enter), not to widen the window.

also_accept covers StateManagement (a shared counter left holding a value derived from a stale read) and Correctness, both defensible readings of the same defect at the same location.

Verified by execution: a throwaway integration test drove the two threads deterministically through channels — thread A's closure signalled that it had read the value, thread B ran `add("hits", 5)` to completion while A was parked, and only then was A released to write. Output, with the crate as shipped:

    running 1 test
    start value              = 10
    closure in thread A saw  = 10
    thread B ran add(hits,5) while the closure was running
    expected final value     = 16
    actual final value       = 11

    thread 'an_update_that_overlaps_another_update' (127808) panicked at tests\zz_throwaway.rs:34:5:
    assertion `left == right` failed
      left: 11
     right: 16
    test an_update_that_overlaps_another_update ... FAILED

    test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

The throwaway test was deleted afterwards; `cargo test` on the shipped crate reports `4 passed; 0 failed`.

OVERLAP, recorded rather than hidden. This case shares a defect CLASS with
`c04-counter-lost-update` in the frozen benchmark: both are a non-atomic
read-modify-write under a mutex, and both lose increments. This case's author
was blocked from reading `benchmark/cases/` and could not have known.

Kept, for three reasons. It sits in a separate set and is folded into no
frozen-benchmark figure, so it inflates nothing. The mechanism differs in the
way that matters for a reviewer: `c04` splits a plain load and store, while here
the gap is opened by running a caller-supplied closure outside the critical
section, which is harder to see and is not fixed by simply holding one guard.
And two independent authors reaching for the same class is mild evidence that it
is a common Rust defect rather than a contrivance.

The honest cost of keeping it: `benchmark/holdout2` is independent of this
project's author in its choice of cases, but not fully independent of the frozen
benchmark in mechanism coverage.
